SuperKart Sales Forecasting: Model Building and Deployment

Approach: full-code. The notebook covers EDA, preprocessing, two tuned ensemble models (Random Forest and Gradient Boosting), model selection, serialization, and deployment of a Flask backend and Streamlit frontend to Hugging Face Spaces.

Target: Product_Store_Sales_Total, the revenue of one product in one store.

Primary metric: RMSE, with R², MAE and MAPE as supporting metrics. - RMSE is in the same unit as revenue, so the error reads directly as rupees/dollars. - It penalises large misses more heavily, which matters for inventory planning (a big under-forecast means stock-outs, a big over-forecast means waste on perishables). - R² shows how much variance the model explains and MAPE gives the relative error, which is easier to explain to business stakeholders.

Contents

  1. Problem statement and metric choice
  2. Libraries and data loading
  3. Data overview

  6. Model building (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting)

  8. Model comparison, final selection, serialization
  9. Deployment: Flask backend, Streamlit frontend, Hugging Face Spaces
  10. Actionable insights and recommendations

Observations - 8,763 rows and 12 columns: 5 numeric and 7 categorical. - There are no missing values and no duplicate rows. - Product_Sugar_Content has an inconsistent label: reg and Regular describe the same category. Fixed in preprocessing. - There are only 4 stores (OUT001 to OUT004) and every store has a single type, size, city tier and establishment year. The store attributes are therefore fully collinear (each store is its own combination), which limits how much each attribute's individual effect can be isolated. - Product_Id is unique per row, so it is not a usable feature by itself, but its two-letter prefix (FD, NC, DR) is a compact product family. - Sales average about 3,464 with a maximum of 8,000 and a minimum of 33.

Insights from EDA - MRP is the strongest driver of sales (correlation 0.79), followed by product weight (0.74). Product_Allocated_Area has essentially no linear relationship with sales (about 0.00). - Store type matters most, and it is entangled with city tier and size. Average sales per product: Departmental Store (OUT003, Tier 1) about 4,947; Supermarket Type1 (OUT001, Tier 2, High size) about 3,924; Supermarket Type2 (OUT004, Tier 2) about 3,299; Food Mart (OUT002, Tier 3, Small) about 1,763. - OUT004 earns roughly half of total revenue (about 15.4M of 30.4M) through volume (4,676 product listings) even though its per-product average is only mid-range. OUT002 is the weakest on both counts. - Per-product averages are nearly identical across product types (about 3,430 to 3,530) and across sugar labels (about 3,440 to 3,500). Category revenue differences come from how many products are stocked, not from higher value per product.

Data Preprocessing

Feature engineering

In [14]:
# 1) Fix the inconsistent sugar label
df["Product_Sugar_Content"] = df["Product_Sugar_Content"].replace({"reg": "Regular"})

# 2) Product_Id prefix -> product family (FD = food, NC = non-consumable, DR = drinks)
df["Product_Id_char"] = df["Product_Id"].str[:2]

# 3) Store age instead of raw establishment year (a more meaningful, model-friendly quantity)
REFERENCE_YEAR = 2025
df["Store_Age_Years"] = REFERENCE_YEAR - df["Store_Establishment_Year"]

# 4) Perishable vs non-perishable grouping of the 16 product types
perishables = ["Dairy", "Meat", "Fruits and Vegetables", "Breakfast", "Breads", "Seafood", "Frozen Foods"]
df["Product_Type_Category"] = np.where(df["Product_Type"].isin(perishables), "Perishables", "Non Perishables")

df[["Product_Id", "Product_Id_char", "Store_Establishment_Year", "Store_Age_Years", "Product_Type", "Product_Type_Category"]].head()
Product_Id Product_Id_char Store_Establishment_Year Store_Age_Years Product_Type Product_Type_Category
0 FD6114 FD 2009 16 Frozen Foods Perishables
1 FD7839 FD 1999 26 Dairy Perishables
2 FD5075 FD 1987 38 Canned Non Perishables
3 FD8233 FD 1987 38 Baking Goods Non Perishables
4 NC1180 NC 1998 27 Health and Hygiene Non Perishables

Rationale - Product_Id is dropped because it is unique per row; its prefix keeps the useful family signal. - Store_Establishment_Year is replaced by Store_Age_Years, which keeps the model from tying itself to a calendar year. - Store_Id is dropped because the store attributes (type, size, tier, age) already describe each store completely, and keeping the ID would let the model memorise 4 stores. - The perishables grouping plus the 16-level Product_Type would be redundant for a compact API, so the deployed feature set keeps the 2-level Product_Type_Category and the ID prefix. This is also the schema of the provided Batch_Data_SuperKart.csv.

Outlier detection and treatment

In [15]:
for c in num_cols:
    q1, q3 = df[c].quantile([0.25, 0.75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    n = ((df[c] < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (df[c] > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum()
    print(f"{c:28s} outliers: {n:4d} ({100 * n / len(df):.1f}%)")

Product_Weight               outliers:   54 (0.6%)
Product_Allocated_Area       outliers:  104 (1.2%)
Product_MRP                  outliers:   57 (0.7%)
Product_Store_Sales_Total    outliers:  119 (1.4%)

No outlier treatment. Outliers are 1 to 1.2% of rows, the flagged values are plausible (heavy products, premium prices, high-selling items), and the models used (tree ensembles) are insensitive to extreme values because they split on thresholds. Capping would hide real high-revenue cases the business wants forecast accurately.

Preparing train and test sets

In [16]:
features = ["Product_Weight", "Product_Sugar_Content", "Product_Allocated_Area", "Product_MRP",
            "Store_Size", "Store_Location_City_Type", "Store_Type",
            "Product_Id_char", "Store_Age_Years", "Product_Type_Category"]

X = df[features]
y = df[target]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

Train: (7010, 10)  Test: (1753, 10)

Preprocessing pipeline for encoding categorical features

In [17]:
categorical_features = X.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns.tolist()
numeric_features = X.select_dtypes(include="number").columns.tolist()
print("Categorical:", categorical_features)
print("Numeric:", numeric_features)

# handle_unknown='ignore' lets the deployed API score categories never seen in training
# (for example a new store type) without crashing.
preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
    remainder="passthrough",   # numeric columns pass through; scaling is unnecessary for tree models
)

Categorical: ['Product_Sugar_Content', 'Store_Size', 'Store_Location_City_Type', 'Store_Type', 'Product_Id_char', 'Product_Type_Category']
Numeric: ['Product_Weight', 'Product_Allocated_Area', 'Product_MRP', 'Store_Age_Years']

Model Building

Functions for model evaluation

In [18]:
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n, k = predictors.shape
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))

def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    pred = model.predict(predictors)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "RMSE": mean_squared_error(target, pred) ** 0.5,
        "MAE": mean_absolute_error(target, pred),
        "R-squared": r2_score(target, pred),
        "Adj. R-squared": adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred),
        "MAPE": mean_absolute_percentage_error(target, pred),
    }, index=[0])

Two base models inside pipelines

The two models are Random Forest (bagging of deep trees, robust and low-variance) and Gradient Boosting (sequential trees that correct earlier errors). Each sits in a pipeline with the preprocessing step.

In [19]:
rf_pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, RandomForestRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1))
gb_pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE))
rf_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
gb_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

rf_train, rf_test = model_performance_regression(rf_pipe, X_train, y_train), model_performance_regression(rf_pipe, X_test, y_test)
gb_train, gb_test = model_performance_regression(gb_pipe, X_train, y_train), model_performance_regression(gb_pipe, X_test, y_test)
print("Random Forest - train"); display(rf_train)
print("Random Forest - test");  display(rf_test)
print("Gradient Boosting - train"); display(gb_train)
print("Gradient Boosting - test");  display(gb_test)

Comments on the base models (values from the run used to write this notebook; a rerun reproduces them because random_state=42) - Random Forest: train RMSE about 107 (R² 0.990) versus test RMSE about 286 (R² 0.928). The gap shows clear overfitting, but test performance is already strong. - Gradient Boosting: train RMSE about 295 (R² 0.923) versus test RMSE about 309 (R² 0.917). It is much better balanced between train and test but slightly less accurate on the test set. - Both explain more than 91% of the variance, which fits the strong MRP and weight signals seen in the EDA.

Model Performance Improvement: Hyperparameter Tuning

Tuning is done with 3-fold cross-validated grid search on the training set, optimising RMSE.

In [20]:
rf_grid = GridSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(preprocessor, RandomForestRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)),
    param_grid={
        "randomforestregressor__n_estimators": [100, 200],
        "randomforestregressor__max_depth": [8, None],
        "randomforestregressor__min_samples_leaf": [1, 3],   # larger leaves counter the overfitting seen above
    },
    cv=3, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1)
rf_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
rf_tuned = rf_grid.best_estimator_
print("Best RF params:", rf_grid.best_params_)

rf_tuned_train, rf_tuned_test = model_performance_regression(rf_tuned, X_train, y_train), model_performance_regression(rf_tuned, X_test, y_test)
print("Tuned Random Forest - train"); display(rf_tuned_train)
print("Tuned Random Forest - test");  display(rf_tuned_test)

Comments on the tuned models - Tuned Random Forest (200 trees, unrestricted depth, min_samples_leaf=3): test RMSE improves from about 286 to about 279 (R² 0.932, MAPE about 3.8%). Train RMSE rises from about 107 to about 198, so the train/test gap shrinks sharply and the model generalises better. - Tuned Gradient Boosting (learning rate 0.1, depth 3, 200 trees): test RMSE improves from about 309 to about 303 (R² 0.920, MAPE about 4.7%). - Both models gain from tuning, but the Random Forest gains more and stays ahead.

Model Performance Comparison, Final Model Selection, and Serialization

In [22]:
def row(name, tr, te):
    return {"Model": name, "Train RMSE": tr.RMSE[0], "Test RMSE": te.RMSE[0], "Test MAE": te.MAE[0],
            "Test R-squared": te["R-squared"][0], "Test MAPE": te.MAPE[0]}

comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    row("Random Forest (base)", rf_train, rf_test),
    row("Gradient Boosting (base)", gb_train, gb_test),
    row("Random Forest (tuned)", rf_tuned_train, rf_tuned_test),
    row("Gradient Boosting (tuned)", gb_tuned_train, gb_tuned_test),
]).set_index("Model").round(4)

Final model: tuned Random Forest. - It has the lowest test RMSE (about 279 versus about 303 for tuned Gradient Boosting), the lowest MAE, the highest R² (0.932) and the lowest MAPE (about 3.8%). - After tuning its train/test gap is moderate, so the accuracy is not just memorisation. - Its errors are small relative to revenue: a typical product-store forecast is off by about 4%.

# Feature importance of the final model (aggregated back to original columns)
rf = best_model.steps[-1][1]
names = best_model.steps[0][1].get_feature_names_out()
imp = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=names).sort_values(ascending=False).head(12)
imp.plot(kind="barh", figsize=(8, 5)).invert_yaxis(); plt.title("Top 12 feature importances"); plt.show()

Deployment: Backend (Flask API)

The backend exposes: - GET / health check - POST /v1/predict single prediction (JSON body) - POST /v1/predictbatch batch predictions (CSV upload)

In [27]:
%%writefile backend_files/app.py
# Flask backend for the SuperKart sales forecasting model
import joblib
import pandas as pd
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask("SuperKart Sales Predictor")

# Load the serialized pipeline (preprocessing + tuned model)
model = joblib.load("SuperKart_model_v1_0.joblib")

FEATURES = [
    "Product_Weight", "Product_Sugar_Content", "Product_Allocated_Area", "Product_MRP",
    "Store_Size", "Store_Location_City_Type", "Store_Type",
    "Product_Id_char", "Store_Age_Years", "Product_Type_Category",
]


@app.get("/")
def home():
    return "Welcome to the SuperKart Sales Forecast API!"


@app.post("/v1/predict")
def predict():
    """Single prediction: expects one JSON object with the model features."""
    data = request.get_json(force=True)
    missing = [f for f in FEATURES if f not in data]
    if missing:
        return jsonify({"error": f"Missing fields: {missing}"}), 400
    row = pd.DataFrame([{f: data[f] for f in FEATURES}])
    pred = float(model.predict(row)[0])
    return jsonify({"Predicted_Sales": round(pred, 2)})


@app.post("/v1/predictbatch")
def predict_batch():
    """Batch prediction: expects a CSV file upload under the key 'file'."""
    if "file" not in request.files:
        return jsonify({"error": "Upload a CSV under the key 'file'"}), 400
    df = pd.read_csv(request.files["file"])
    missing = [f for f in FEATURES if f not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        return jsonify({"error": f"Missing columns: {missing}"}), 400
    preds = model.predict(df[FEATURES]).round(2).tolist()
    return jsonify({"Predicted_Sales": preds})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=7860, debug=False)

%%writefile frontend_files/app.py
# Streamlit frontend for the SuperKart sales forecasting model
import os
import requests
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

# Set BACKEND_URL as a Space variable, or edit the default below
BACKEND_URL = os.getenv("BACKEND_URL", "https://<your-username>-superkart-backend.hf.space").rstrip("/")

st.set_page_config(page_title="SuperKart Sales Forecast", layout="centered")
st.title("SuperKart Sales Forecast")
st.write("Predict the total sales of a product in a store, one at a time or in bulk.")

st.subheader("Online prediction (single)")
c1, c2 = st.columns(2)
with c1:
    product_weight = st.number_input("Product Weight", 0.0, 50.0, 12.5, 0.01)
    sugar = st.selectbox("Sugar Content", ["Low Sugar", "Regular", "No Sugar"])
    area = st.number_input("Allocated Display Area (ratio)", 0.0, 1.0, 0.07, 0.001, format="%.3f")
    mrp = st.number_input("Product MRP", 0.0, 500.0, 147.0, 0.01)
    id_char = st.selectbox("Product ID prefix", ["FD", "NC", "DR"])
    category = st.selectbox("Product Type Category", ["Perishables", "Non Perishables"])
with c2:
    store_size = st.selectbox("Store Size", ["Small", "Medium", "High"])
    city = st.selectbox("City Tier", ["Tier 1", "Tier 2", "Tier 3"])
    store_type = st.selectbox("Store Type", ["Supermarket Type1", "Supermarket Type2", "Departmental Store", "Food Mart"])
    store_age = st.number_input("Store Age (years)", 0, 100, 16, 1)

if st.button("Predict Sales"):
    payload = {
        "Product_Weight": product_weight, "Product_Sugar_Content": sugar,
        "Product_Allocated_Area": area, "Product_MRP": mrp, "Store_Size": store_size,
        "Store_Location_City_Type": city, "Store_Type": store_type,
        "Product_Id_char": id_char, "Store_Age_Years": store_age,
        "Product_Type_Category": category,
    }
    try:
        r = requests.post(f"{BACKEND_URL}/v1/predict", json=payload, timeout=60)
        if r.ok:
            st.success(f"Predicted sales: {r.json()['Predicted_Sales']:,.2f}")
        else:
            st.error(f"Backend error {r.status_code}: {r.text}")
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        st.error(f"Could not reach the backend: {e}")

st.subheader("Batch prediction")
up = st.file_uploader("Upload a CSV file", type=["csv"])
if up is not None and st.button("Predict for Batch"):
    try:
        r = requests.post(f"{BACKEND_URL}/v1/predictbatch", files={"file": (up.name, up.getvalue(), "text/csv")}, timeout=120)
        if r.ok:
            up.seek(0)
            out = pd.read_csv(up)
            out["Predicted_Sales"] = r.json()["Predicted_Sales"]
            st.dataframe(out)
            st.download_button("Download predictions", out.to_csv(index=False), "superkart_predictions.csv", "text/csv")
        else:
            st.error(f"Backend error {r.status_code}: {r.text}")
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        st.error(f"Could not reach the backend: {e}")

Actionable Insights and Recommendations

Insights

  1. The model is accurate enough to plan with. The tuned Random Forest explains about 93% of the variance in product-store sales and is typically within about 4% (MAPE) of the actual value, with an RMSE of about 279 on average sales of about 3,464.
  2. Price is the main revenue driver. MRP (correlation 0.79) and product weight (0.74) explain most of the variation, while shelf area has no meaningful effect on sales.
  3. Store format decides how much each product sells. Average sales per product run from about 4,947 in the Tier 1 Departmental Store to about 1,763 in the Tier 3 Food Mart, a 2.8x gap.
  4. Revenue is concentrated. OUT004 (Supermarket Type2) brings in about half of total revenue through sheer product volume, so any disruption there moves the total forecast a lot.
  5. Product category and sugar label barely change value per product. Category revenue differences come from how many products are stocked.

Recommendations

  1. Use the model for product-level demand and stock planning, and use its predictions as a baseline for procurement volumes per store, prioritising high-MRP and heavy items where the revenue per listing is highest.
  2. Grow the Departmental Store and Tier 1 footprint. They deliver the highest revenue per product; test new formats there before adding more Food Marts.
  3. Review the Food Mart (OUT002). It has the lowest sales per product and the lowest total revenue. Consider a range reset toward higher-MRP items, a format change, or a cost review.
  4. Protect OUT004 with contingency stock and staffing plans because of its half-of-revenue weight, and study what its wide assortment does right so it can be replicated in OUT001.
  5. Do not rely on shelf-space changes to lift sales without a test; the data shows no link between allocated area and revenue.
  6. Perishables: because the forecast is more precise for higher-value items, use tighter forecasts and shorter reorder cycles for perishable, high-MRP products to cut waste.

Limitations and next steps

  • The data has no date or time dimension, so the model predicts revenue for a product-store combination from its attributes; it does not model seasonality or trend. A true next-quarter forecast needs dated sales history (weekly or monthly) and a time-series feature set.
  • With only 4 stores, store attributes cannot be separated from each other, and the model may not generalise to a new store type (the batch file even contains a Supermarket Type3, which the pipeline handles by ignoring the unseen category rather than predicting from it).
  • Retrain periodically and monitor MAPE by store once real forecasts can be compared with actuals.
